liturgical_day: Memorial of Saint Augustine, Bishop and Doctor of the Church
scripture_edition: Douay-AI, modernized from the public-domain Douay-Rheims Bible.
title: Oil for the midnight hour
theme: The lamps are visible, but the hidden oil reveals whether a life is ready for the Bridegroom. Christ calls every disciple to a faith sustained by charity, an inward conscience turned toward God, and good works that cannot be postponed or borrowed at the hour of judgment.
introduction: Jesus places ten virgins on the same road. All are invited, all carry lamps, all await the same bridegroom, and all grow drowsy during the delay. The division appears not in the invitation or even in the sleeping, but in the provision each has made before midnight. The wise carry oil within their vessels; the foolish possess the outward form of readiness without the reserve that can keep its light alive. The Fathers see in this oil the fruit of mercy, the joy of a conscience pleasing to God, and the good works that give substance to confessed faith. These interpretations converge on one sober truth: no outward profession can replace a life inwardly formed by grace and expressed in charity. When the cry comes, the virgins rise together, but the final hour reveals what each has become. The wise cannot transfer their readiness, because judgment concerns the truth of each conscience and the deeds of each life. Nor can the foolish create a history of love once the Bridegroom has arrived and the door has closed. Christ therefore ends not with a timetable but with a command: watch. Christian vigilance is neither panic nor prediction. It is the patient work of keeping the lamp supplied—receiving God’s gifts, practicing mercy, seeking his approval rather than applause, and remaining prepared through the long delay for the joy of the wedding feast.
hero_alt: Ten virgins await the approaching bridegroom at midnight, five holding radiant oil lamps and five facing fading flames, in Byzantine mosaic, stained glass, gold leaf, and restrained luminous geometry
closing: The lamp is what others can see; the vessel is what God sees. It is possible to carry the signs of discipleship while allowing the inner reserve of charity to run dry. Christ’s parable asks us to attend to what cannot be borrowed at the last moment: a conscience trained to seek God’s pleasure, habits of mercy formed through repeated choices, and a faith made living in deeds. The delay of the Bridegroom is not permission to drift. It is mercy, giving time for grace to take root and for love to become steady. Begin with the oil needed today. Offer the help you have postponed. Pray where only the Father sees. Repair the relationship that pride has left unattended. Let worship issue in service, and let each good work be done for God rather than for an audience. We do not keep watch by refusing ordinary rest; all ten virgins slept. We keep watch by being ready when we are awakened. The midnight cry will not create a new heart but disclose the one we have allowed grace to form. Keep the vessel full, the lamp trimmed, and the heart turned toward Christ. Then his arrival will not be an interruption to fear, but the fulfillment of the meeting for which the whole life has been waiting.

verses.text: Then the kingdom of heaven shall be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride.
verses.author: St Jerome
verses.insight: The invitation extends beyond one state of life to the whole human race. Every person is summoned to prepare for the coming of the Bridegroom.
verses.commentary: Jerome cautions against restricting the parable to consecrated virgins alone. Although its imagery includes bodily virginity, the surrounding discourse concerns the judgment that awaits all humanity. The ten virgins therefore represent the human race called to meet Christ, not a narrow spiritual class. Their common procession shows the breadth of the invitation: each life moves toward an encounter with the Bridegroom. The decisive question will not be whether someone outwardly resembled the figures in the parable, but whether the whole person was prepared for the Lord who comes.
verses.source_label: St Jerome, Commentary on Matthew, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:1–5

verses.text: Five of them were foolish, and five were wise.
verses.author: Origen
verses.insight: Right profession and righteous living belong together. Wisdom prepares faith through good works, while folly leaves confession without the life it requires.
verses.commentary: Origen distinguishes the two groups by the union—or separation—of belief and conduct. The wise both believe rightly and live righteously. The foolish profess faith in Jesus, yet do not prepare themselves for salvation through good works. Their shared virginity and lamps show that outward belonging does not erase this moral difference. Wisdom is not mere information about the Bridegroom; it orders life toward meeting him. Folly can speak the language of faith while neglecting the deeds by which faith becomes ready, durable, and responsive to the grace it has received.
verses.source_label: Origen, Commentary on Matthew, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:1–5

verses.text: But the five foolish, having taken their lamps, did not take oil with them.
verses.author: St Jerome
verses.insight: A lamp of confession is not enough without the oil of virtue. Faith must be adorned and sustained by the good works it is meant to produce.
verses.commentary: Jerome reads the oil as the ornament of good works added to faith. The foolish virgins appear to confess the same faith as the wise, for they also carry lamps, but they neglect the virtues that would keep those lamps burning. Their failure is therefore not lack of an outward sign; it is lack of inwardly prepared substance. Christ warns against treating confession as self-sufficient when conduct contradicts or starves it. The lamp is meant to shine, and it can endure only when a life of virtue supplies what the visible profession announces.
verses.source_label: St Jerome, Commentary on Matthew, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:1–5

verses.text: But the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps.
verses.author: St Augustine of Hippo
verses.insight: The wise carry the joy of good works within the conscience. Their gladness comes from pleasing God, not from being praised by observers.
verses.commentary: Augustine understands the oil as holy joy stored in the heart and conscience. Good works give lasting gladness when they are done before God and for his pleasure, rather than performed to win human applause. The vessel is inward because the motive of a deed cannot be secured by appearances. A person may carry a bright lamp before others and still lack the oil that endures when their praise disappears. The wise examine their work before God, keeping within themselves the joy of a conscience directed toward him. That hidden reserve sustains the visible light.
verses.source_label: St Augustine of Hippo, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:1–5

verses.text: As the bridegroom delayed, they all grew drowsy and slept.
verses.author: St Gregory the Great
verses.insight: Both wise and foolish pass through death while the Lord’s coming seems delayed. What distinguishes them is the readiness carried into that sleep.
verses.commentary: Gregory interprets sleep as death and the preceding drowsiness as the weakening that often comes through illness before death. The verse does not condemn the wise for sleeping, since all ten virgins share this human end while awaiting the resurrection. Its seriousness lies in what each carries when sleep arrives. Mortality overtakes both the visibly prepared and the visibly unprepared; death itself does not supply the missing oil. The Bridegroom’s delay therefore makes present preparation more urgent, because the soul must enter its final sleep with the substance of a faithful life already held within.
verses.source_label: St Gregory the Great, Homilies on the Gospels, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:1–5

verses.text: At midnight a cry was made: ‘Behold, the bridegroom comes; go out to meet him.’
verses.author: St Jerome
verses.insight: Christ’s coming breaks into the hour of deepest security. The angelic cry reveals that what seemed delayed was never absent or uncertain.
verses.commentary: Jerome emphasizes the suddenness of midnight, when sleep is deepest and people imagine themselves secure. At that unforeseen hour, Christ’s arrival is proclaimed by the shout of angels and the heavenly powers that precede him. The darkness does not mean the Bridegroom has lost his way; it reveals how little human expectation governs his coming. The cry awakens everyone at once and turns waiting into encounter. Because no one can arrange the hour, readiness must be formed before the announcement sounds. The summons will be joyful to those whose lamps can answer it with light.
verses.source_label: St Jerome, Commentary on Matthew, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:6–9

verses.text: Then all those virgins arose and trimmed their lamps.
verses.author: St Augustine of Hippo
verses.insight: The awakened virgins prepare to give an account of their deeds. Judgment brings every work into the light for which it was truly done.
verses.commentary: Augustine says that trimming the lamps means preparing to render an account of one’s deeds. The midnight cry does not merely wake bodies; it brings each life before the truth of judgment. All the virgins rise and examine their lamps, because all must answer for what their visible works contain. Trimming cannot manufacture oil that was never stored, but it exposes whether the flame has a lasting source. The image calls Christians to examine their deeds now, while repentance and growth remain possible, so that the final accounting reveals a conscience already oriented toward God.
verses.source_label: St Augustine of Hippo, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:6–9

verses.text: The foolish said to the wise, ‘Give us some of your oil, for our lamps have gone out.’
verses.author: St Gregory the Great
verses.insight: Works done for appearance lose their brightness before the Judge. When outward approval vanishes, an empty conscience cannot borrow another person’s witness.
verses.commentary: Gregory explains that the foolish lamps go out because works that looked bright before human observers are dark within when the Judge comes. Finding no testimony in their own consciences, the foolish seek it from their neighbors, as though another person’s approval could establish the truth of their lives before God. Their request reveals the habit that emptied them: they depended on witnesses who saw appearances rather than on the Lord who sees the heart. At judgment, borrowed reputation cannot become inward charity. The soul needs the oil of deeds sincerely done before God, stored while there is time to act.
verses.source_label: St Gregory the Great, Homilies on the Gospels, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:6–9

verses.text: The wise answered, saying, ‘Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you; go rather to those who sell, and buy for yourselves.’
verses.author: St John Chrysostom
verses.insight: At judgment, even the merciful cannot stand as patrons for lives left empty of mercy. Readiness is personal because each life must answer through its own deeds.
verses.commentary: Chrysostom insists that the wise refuse neither from hardness nor from lack of mercy. Indeed, mercy is precisely what made them ready. They cannot lend their oil because, on the day of judgment, no person can serve as patron for someone betrayed by his or her own works. Charity offered during life can aid a neighbor, but one person’s history of love cannot be transferred into another conscience at the end. The reply therefore urges present responsibility: receive help now, learn mercy now, and practice it now, while the poor and every opportunity for loving action are still near.
verses.source_label: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:6–9

verses.text: While they went to buy, the bridegroom came; those who were ready entered with him into the marriage, and the door was shut.
verses.author: St Jerome
verses.insight: The arrival of judgment ends the season for forming a life of righteousness. Those already prepared enter the joy for which their readiness was shaped.
verses.commentary: Jerome teaches that after judgment there is no further opportunity to begin good works or acquire righteousness; this is the force of the shut door. The foolish turn toward preparation only when the season for preparation has ended. Meanwhile, those already ready enter the marriage with the Bridegroom. The image is not meant to make grace scarce, but to show that time and moral choice are real. God’s mercy gives the present moment for repentance and faithful action. Once earthly life reaches its final accounting, desire for a different past cannot replace the deeds that love could have done.
verses.source_label: St Jerome, Commentary on Matthew, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:10–13

verses.text: At last the other virgins also came, saying, ‘Lord, Lord, open to us.’
verses.author: St Jerome
verses.insight: Calling Jesus ‘Lord’ is a true confession, yet words cannot replace the obedience they profess. Faith of the mouth must be joined to works of the life.
verses.commentary: Jerome recognizes that the repeated title ‘Lord, Lord’ expresses a worthy confession of faith. Yet he asks what such confession can accomplish when a person’s works have denied the one named by the lips. The foolish virgins know whom to address, but their late appeal exposes the distance between their words and their lives. Christ does not oppose faith and deeds; he reveals that genuine confession seeks embodiment in obedience and charity. The verse therefore warns against relying on religious language as a substitute for conversion. To call Christ Lord is to let his lordship shape how one lives.
verses.source_label: St Jerome, Commentary on Matthew, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:10–13

verses.text: But he answered, ‘Amen I say to you, I do not know you.’
verses.author: St Augustine of Hippo
verses.insight: A life aimed at human praise remains unknown to the joy of God. The Bridegroom’s verdict discloses the motive that outward works had concealed.
verses.commentary: Augustine connects the Bridegroom’s answer to the foolish virgins’ pursuit of human approval. They attempted what resembled obedience, but not before God; their aim was to please other people. Divine wisdom does not admit such a life into the joy it never truly sought. The words ‘I do not know you’ therefore expose more than missing external achievements. They reveal a heart whose works were directed toward an audience rather than toward communion with God. Before judgment, divine mercy remains open beyond measure. Afterward, the verdict names the settled truth of what the person chose to love.
verses.source_label: St Augustine of Hippo, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:10–13

verses.text: Watch therefore, because you know neither the day nor the hour.
verses.author: St Augustine of Hippo
verses.insight: We know neither the hour of Christ’s final coming nor the hour of our own death. Readiness for the personal summons prepares us also for the universal one.
verses.commentary: Augustine applies Christ’s command to two hidden moments: the future coming of the Bridegroom and each person’s own falling asleep in death. Neither hour is ours to know. If the soul is prepared when earthly life ends, it will also be prepared when the final voice awakens all humanity. Watchfulness is therefore not an attempt to calculate the end, but a way of inhabiting the present before God. Each day becomes time to repent, to practice mercy, and to keep faith alive in love, so that any hour may find the lamp supplied.
verses.source_label: St Augustine of Hippo, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 25:10–13
